Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Disclosed here are inventive systems and methods for a powertrain of an electric vehicle (EV) having a continuously variable transmission (CVT) coupled to an electric drive motor, wherein a control system is configured to control the CVT and/or the drive motor to optimize various efficiencies associated with the EV and/or its subsystems. A control system is configured to operate the EV in an economy mode. Operating in said mode, the control system simultaneously manages the CVT and the drive motor to optimize the range of the EV. The control system can be configured to manage the current provided to the drive motor, as well as adjust a transmission speed ratio of the CVT. Other modes of operation are also possible. The control system can be configured to manage the power to the drive motor and adjust the transmission speed ratio of the CVT taking into account battery voltage, throttle position, and transmission speed ratio, for example.

The disclosure relates to an electric-vehicle powertrain having an electric traction motor coupled to one or more drive wheels through a continuously variable transmission (CVT). A control system coordinates operation of the motor and the transmission so that they function as an integrated propulsion system rather than as independently controlled components. The control system may receive operating information including motor current, battery voltage, accelerator or throttle position, vehicle speed, motor speed, transmission input and output speed, and the current transmission ratio. Based on these inputs, the controller determines the torque and speed required to satisfy the driver’s demand and selects an appropriate motor operating point and CVT ratio.

In an economy operating mode, the controller adjusts the transmission ratio while regulating motor current, torque, or speed to maintain the motor, battery, and transmission near efficient operating regions. For example, the CVT can vary its ratio so that the motor operates at a speed and load associated with relatively high efficiency, while the motor controller supplies only the electrical power needed to produce the requested vehicle performance. Battery-voltage and motor-current measurements can be used to estimate power consumption, account for changing battery conditions, and prevent operation beyond allowable electrical or mechanical limits. Coordinating these functions reduces avoidable energy losses and can increase the distance the vehicle travels on a given battery charge.

The control system may also provide operating modes other than economy mode. Such modes can prioritize acceleration, responsiveness, grade-climbing capability, speed regulation, regenerative braking, or protection of powertrain components. Driver-selected commands and detected operating conditions may be used to transition between modes, with corresponding changes to motor control and transmission-ratio scheduling. In this manner, the disclosed system balances driver demand, vehicle performance, component constraints, and energy efficiency while providing flexible control of an electric-vehicle powertrain.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a patent-style abstract describing an electric vehicle powertrain with a CVT and a control system that optimizes efficiency and driving range.
counterfactuals.output: An electric vehicle powertrain includes an electric traction motor, an energy storage system, a continuously variable transmission (CVT) operatively coupled between the traction motor and one or more drive wheels, and a control system configured to coordinate operation of the traction motor and the CVT. The control system determines a requested wheel torque based on driver input and vehicle operating conditions and selects a CVT ratio that causes the traction motor to operate at a target speed and torque within an efficiency-optimized region. The target operating point may be determined using motor efficiency data, transmission losses, battery state of charge, thermal limits, vehicle speed, road grade, predicted route conditions, and regenerative braking availability. The control system adjusts motor torque and CVT ratio in real time while maintaining desired vehicle performance and drivability. During deceleration, the control system controls the CVT ratio to increase recoverable regenerative energy subject to traction, battery charging, and component constraints. By optimizing combined efficiencies of the traction motor, CVT, and energy storage system over a drive cycle, the powertrain reduces electrical energy consumption and increases vehicle driving range.

counterfactuals.output: The invention is an electric-vehicle control system that coordinates traction-motor current with a continuously variable transmission’s ratio during an economy mode. Based on driver demand, vehicle speed, and operating conditions, the controller selects both the motor torque/current and transmission ratio to keep the motor near a high-efficiency operating region while still providing the required wheel torque. By shifting ratio and adjusting current together—rather than controlling them independently—the system reduces electrical energy consumption, limits unnecessary current, and extends driving range without compromising basic drivability.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a technical disclosure for an electric vehicle system that adjusts drive-motor power and CVT speed ratio based on battery voltage, throttle position, and current transmission ratio.
counterfactuals.output:
# Technical Disclosure

## Title

**Electric Vehicle Propulsion Control Using Battery Voltage, Throttle Position, and Continuously Variable Transmission Ratio**

## 1. Technical Field

This disclosure relates to electric vehicle propulsion systems and, more particularly, to coordinated control of electric drive-motor power and a continuously variable transmission (“CVT”) based on battery voltage, operator throttle position, and a current CVT speed ratio.

## 2. Background

An electric traction motor coupled to a CVT can operate over a wider range of vehicle speeds than a fixed-ratio electric drive. The CVT ratio may be adjusted to keep the motor near an efficient or high-torque operating region. However, a requested motor power level may not always be compatible with the instantaneous battery condition or transmission ratio.

For example, battery terminal voltage may decrease due to low state of charge, low temperature, battery aging, or voltage sag under load. If a controller continues to command motor power based only on throttle position, battery current can increase as voltage decreases, potentially causing further voltage sag, battery protection events, or abrupt loss of propulsion. In addition, the current CVT ratio influences motor speed, motor torque, available wheel torque, and the ratio adjustment needed to satisfy a driver request.

A need therefore exists for a propulsion controller that jointly determines motor power and CVT ratio using battery voltage, throttle position, and the current transmission ratio. Coordinated control can preserve battery voltage, limit electrical and mechanical loads, improve drivability, and reduce unnecessary CVT ratio changes.

## 3. Summary

A vehicle propulsion system includes:

- a rechargeable battery;
- an electric drive motor;
- an inverter electrically coupling the battery to the motor;
- a CVT mechanically coupling the motor to one or more driven wheels;
- a battery-voltage sensor;
- a throttle-position sensor;
- a transmission-ratio sensor or ratio estimator; and
- a controller configured to regulate motor output and CVT ratio.

The controller receives:

1. a measured or estimated battery voltage;
2. a throttle-position signal representing operator propulsion demand; and
3. a current CVT speed ratio.

The controller determines a requested propulsion power from the throttle position and modifies that requested power according to battery voltage and the current CVT ratio. The controller also determines a target CVT ratio using the same inputs. Motor power and transmission ratio may therefore be coordinated rather than controlled independently.

When battery voltage is above a first threshold, the controller may provide a normal motor-power command and select a CVT ratio based primarily on throttle demand, vehicle speed, and motor efficiency. When battery voltage decreases below the first threshold, the controller may reduce allowable motor power and command a CVT ratio that reduces battery current, maintains the motor within a permitted speed/torque region, or provides a desired amount of wheel torque with reduced electrical stress. When voltage decreases below a lower threshold, the controller may impose a more restrictive power limit and inhibit ratio changes that would increase battery loading.

The current transmission ratio is used to determine whether a target ratio is feasible, calculate available wheel torque, limit the rate of ratio change, and avoid discontinuities in motor torque during ratio transitions.

## 4. System Architecture

### 4.1 Propulsion Components

An example system includes:

- battery pack having a nominal DC voltage;
- battery-management system (“BMS”);
- DC-link capacitor and inverter;
- permanent-magnet, induction, switched-reluctance, or other electric traction motor;
- belt, chain, toroidal, hydrostatic, or other continuously variable transmission;
- final drive and driven wheels;
- CVT actuator;
- accelerator or throttle input device; and
- vehicle control unit.

The CVT speed ratio may be defined as:

\[
R_{cvt}=\frac{\omega_m}{\omega_o}
\]

where \(\omega_m\) is motor or CVT input speed and \(\omega_o\) is CVT output speed. A higher numerical ratio therefore corresponds to higher motor speed for a given output speed. The disclosed control also applies if the transmission uses the reciprocal ratio convention.

### 4.2 Input Signals

The controller may receive or derive:

- battery terminal voltage \(V_b\);
- filtered battery voltage \(\bar V_b\);
- battery current \(I_b\);
- throttle position \(T\), such as a normalized value from zero to one;
- current CVT ratio \(R_{act}\);
- motor speed \(\omega_m\);
- motor torque;
- vehicle speed;
- CVT input and output speeds;
- battery state of charge and temperature;
- motor and inverter temperatures;
- CVT temperature and actuator status; and
- braking or regenerative-power requests.

Battery voltage may be measured directly, supplied by the BMS, or estimated from cell voltages and electrical models. Current CVT ratio may be measured from pulley positions, determined from input and output speeds, or estimated from an actuator model.

## 5. Control Method

### 5.1 Throttle-Based Power Request

The controller converts throttle position into an unmodified propulsion-power request:

\[
P_{drv}=f_T(T,v)
\]

where \(v\) is vehicle speed. In a simplified implementation:

\[
P_{drv}=T P_{max}
\]

where \(P_{max}\) is the nominal maximum propulsion power. A nonlinear throttle map may provide finer control at low throttle positions.

### 5.2 Voltage-Dependent Power Limit

The controller determines an allowable battery or motor power as a function of battery voltage:

\[
P_V=f_V(V_b)
\]

For example:

\[
P_V=
\begin{cases}
P_{max}, & V_b \ge V_H\\
P_{min}+(P_{max}-P_{min})\dfrac{V_b-V_L}{V_H-V_L},
& V_L<V_b<V_H\\
P_{min}, & V_b\le V_L
\end{cases}
\]

where \(V_H\) is a normal-operation threshold, \(V_L\) is a low-voltage threshold, and \(P_{min}\) is a reduced power limit. Below a critical voltage \(V_C\), propulsion may be further reduced or disabled.

In another implementation, allowable power is calculated from a current limit:

\[
P_V=\eta_e V_b I_{lim}
\]

where \(\eta_e\) represents inverter and motor efficiency and \(I_{lim}\) may be supplied by the BMS.

### 5.3 Ratio-Dependent Power Limit

The controller determines a ratio-dependent limit:

\[
P_R=f_R(R_{act},\omega_m,v)
\]

The ratio-dependent limit may account for:

- maximum motor torque at the current motor speed;
- maximum motor or CVT input speed;
- CVT torque capacity;
- belt or chain clamping-force limits;
- ratio-dependent transmission efficiency; and
- expected ratio-change time.

An available wheel-torque estimate may be calculated as:

\[
\tau_{w,avail}
=
\tau_{m,avail} R_{act} R_f \eta_{cvt}
\]

where \(R_f\) is a final-drive ratio and \(\eta_{cvt}\) is transmission efficiency.

### 5.4 Motor-Power Command

The commanded motor power may be:

\[
P_{cmd}=\min(P_{drv},P_V,P_R,P_{thermal})
\]

where \(P_{thermal}\) is an optional temperature-dependent limit.

Alternatively, a continuous derating factor may be used:

\[
P_{cmd}=P_{drv}\,K_V(V_b)\,K_R(R_{act},T)
\]

where \(K_V\) and \(K_R\) range from zero to one.

The motor-torque command may then be calculated as:

\[
\tau_{m,cmd}
=
\frac{P_{cmd}}{\max(|\omega_m|,\omega_\epsilon)}
\]

subject to motor, inverter, battery, and CVT torque limits. At low motor speed, a separate torque map may be used to avoid division by a near-zero speed.

### 5.5 Target CVT Ratio

The controller determines a target ratio:

\[
R_{tgt}=f_{ratio}(V_b,T,R_{act},v)
\]

At moderate or high battery voltage, \(R_{tgt}\) may place the motor near an efficiency-optimal operating point. At reduced battery voltage, the target ratio may be modified to reduce battery current or avoid a high motor-torque condition.

An example target motor speed is:

\[
\omega_{m,tgt}
=
\omega_{base}(P_{cmd})
+
\Delta \omega_T(T)
+
\Delta \omega_V(V_b)
\]

The corresponding target ratio is:

\[
R_{tgt}
=
\operatorname{clamp}
\left(
\frac{\omega_{m,tgt}}{\omega_o},
R_{min},
R_{max}
\right)
\]

At high throttle, the controller may select a higher numerical ratio to increase wheel torque while limiting motor torque, provided that the resulting motor speed and CVT loading remain within limits. At low or moderate throttle, the controller may select a ratio associated with high motor and transmission efficiency. During low-voltage operation, the ratio may be selected to minimize estimated battery current:

\[
R_{tgt}
=
\arg\min_R
\left[
I_{b,est}(P_{wheel,req},R,V_b)
+
\lambda_1(R-R_{act})^2
+
\lambda_2 L_{cvt}(R)
\right]
\]

where the second term penalizes excessive ratio movement and \(L_{cvt}\) represents CVT loading or loss.

### 5.6 Coordinated Transition Control

Before or during a ratio change, the controller may temporarily modify motor torque to reduce shift shock or CVT stress. A ratio-rate command may be expressed as:

\[
\dot R_{cmd}
=
\operatorname{sat}
\left(
K_R(R_{tgt}-R_{act}),
-\dot R_{max},
\dot R_{max}
\right)
\]

The allowable ratio-change rate may decrease when battery voltage is low, throttle demand is changing rapidly, CVT torque is high, or the actual ratio differs significantly from an expected ratio.

Motor power may be coordinated with ratio movement so that wheel torque changes gradually:

\[
\tau_{m,cmd}
=
\frac{\tau_{w,tgt}}
{R_{act}R_f\eta_{cvt}}
\]

As the actual ratio approaches the target ratio, the controller updates the motor torque needed to maintain the desired wheel torque.

## 6. Example Operating Modes

### Normal-Voltage Mode

When battery voltage exceeds a normal threshold:

- motor power is primarily determined from throttle position;
- the ratio is selected for efficiency, performance, or noise;
- full rated propulsion power may be available; and
- ratio changes may occur at a normal rate.

### Voltage-Derating Mode

When battery voltage is between normal and low thresholds:

- allowable motor power is progressively reduced;
- the target ratio is biased toward a motor operating region requiring less battery current for the requested wheel output;
- rapid ratio changes may be limited; and
- filtered voltage and hysteresis prevent repeated switching between modes.

### Low-Voltage Protection Mode

When battery voltage is below the low threshold:

- motor power is restricted to a predetermined minimum or limp-home level;
- the CVT is prevented from selecting a ratio that would cause motor overspeed, excessive motor torque, or excessive transmission input torque;
- throttle commands are rate-limited; and
- propulsion may be disabled if voltage falls below a critical threshold for a specified duration.

### High-Throttle Mode

At high throttle:

- the controller evaluates whether the current ratio can deliver the requested wheel torque;
- motor power is limited to the voltage-dependent limit;
- the CVT is moved toward a torque-multiplying ratio when permissible; and
- motor power may be ramped as the CVT approaches the target ratio.

### Low-Throttle Cruise Mode

At low throttle:

- the target ratio may reduce motor speed and power losses;
- unnecessary ratio movement is suppressed by a deadband; and
- a low-voltage condition may cause modest power derating without a perceptible abrupt change.

## 7. Filtering, Hysteresis, and Diagnostics

Battery voltage may be processed using a low-pass filter, moving average, or model-based estimator. A fast voltage path may detect severe voltage collapse, while a slower path determines sustained derating.

Different entry and exit thresholds may be used:

- enter derating when \(V_b<V_{enter}\);
- exit derating when \(V_b>V_{exit}\); and
- set \(V_{exit}>V_{enter}\).

The controller may compare a commanded ratio with a measured ratio. If the difference remains above a threshold, a CVT fault may be declared and motor power limited according to the actual ratio rather than the commanded ratio.

If the throttle sensor is invalid, the controller may command zero propulsion torque or a restricted fallback torque. If the battery-voltage signal is invalid, a conservative voltage estimate or fixed reduced-power mode may be used.

## 8. Regenerative Operation

The same principles may be applied during regenerative braking. A negative motor-power command may be limited according to battery voltage and current charge acceptance. When battery voltage approaches an upper charging limit, regenerative power may be reduced and the CVT ratio may be adjusted to maintain motor speed within a suitable regenerative region. Friction braking may supply any remaining braking demand.

## 9. Advantages

Potential advantages include:

- reduced risk of battery undervoltage;
- lower peak battery current;
- smoother power derating;
- coordinated motor and CVT operation;
- improved wheel-torque control during ratio changes;
- reduced CVT mechanical stress;
- improved propulsion efficiency; and
- continued limited vehicle operation under low-voltage conditions.

## 10. Example Method

A control cycle may include:

1. measuring battery voltage, throttle position, and current CVT ratio;
2. validating and filtering the measurements;
3. determining a throttle-based propulsion request;
4. determining a voltage-based motor-power limit;
5. determining a ratio-dependent motor-power limit;
6. calculating a commanded motor power from the propulsion request and applicable limits;
7. calculating a target CVT ratio using battery voltage, throttle position, and current ratio;
8. rate-limiting the target ratio or CVT actuator command;
9. coordinating motor torque with the measured ratio during ratio movement;
10. monitoring battery voltage and ratio-tracking performance; and
11. entering a reduced-power or fault mode when a limit or diagnostic condition is met.

## 11. Illustrative Claims

1. **A propulsion system for an electric vehicle**, comprising:  
   a battery;  
   an electric drive motor electrically coupled to the battery;  
   a continuously variable transmission coupling the electric drive motor to a driven wheel;  
   a voltage sensor configured to provide a battery-voltage signal;  
   a throttle sensor configured to provide a throttle-position signal;  
   a ratio sensor or estimator configured to provide a current transmission-ratio signal; and  
   a controller configured to:  
   determine a requested propulsion output based on the throttle-position signal;  
   determine a motor-power command based on the requested propulsion output, the battery-voltage signal, and the current transmission-ratio signal; and  
   determine a target transmission ratio based on the battery-voltage signal, the throttle-position signal, and the current transmission-ratio signal.

2. The propulsion system of claim 1, wherein the controller reduces the motor-power command in response to the battery voltage decreasing below a first voltage threshold.

3. The propulsion system of claim 2, wherein the controller progressively reduces the motor-power command between the first voltage threshold and a second, lower voltage threshold.

4. The propulsion system of claim 1, wherein the controller determines a ratio-dependent motor-power limit based on at least one of motor speed, motor torque capacity, or CVT input-torque capacity at the current transmission ratio.

5. The propulsion system of claim 1, wherein the controller selects the target transmission ratio to reduce estimated battery current while satisfying at least a portion of the requested propulsion output.

6. The propulsion system of claim 1, wherein the controller limits a rate of change of the transmission ratio and adjusts motor torque as the current transmission ratio approaches the target transmission ratio.

7. The propulsion system of claim 1, wherein the controller uses the current transmission ratio, rather than a commanded transmission ratio, to determine an available wheel torque.

8. The propulsion system of claim 1, wherein the controller enters a reduced-power mode when the battery voltage remains below a threshold for a predetermined duration.

9. **A method of controlling an electric vehicle**, comprising:  
   receiving a battery-voltage value, a throttle-position value, and a current continuously variable transmission ratio;  
   determining a driver-requested power from the throttle-position value;  
   determining an allowable motor power from the battery-voltage value and the current continuously variable transmission ratio;  
   commanding the electric motor according to the lesser of the driver-requested power and the allowable motor power; and  
   commanding a target continuously variable transmission ratio determined from the battery-voltage value, the throttle-position value, and the current continuously variable transmission ratio.

10. The method of claim 9, further comprising coordinating motor torque with a measured change in the continuously variable transmission ratio to limit a change in wheel torque.

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe systems and methods for improving EV range by coordinating an electric drive motor with a continuously variable transmission, including multiple operating modes.
counterfactuals.output:
A range-improving electric-vehicle drivetrain can combine an electric traction motor with a continuously variable transmission (CVT) and coordinate both through a supervisory controller. Unlike a fixed-ratio EV drivetrain, the CVT allows vehicle speed and motor speed to be partly decoupled, so the motor can operate more frequently in high-efficiency regions.

## System architecture

The system may include:

- A traction battery and inverter;
- One or more electric drive motors;
- A CVT positioned between the motor and driven wheels;
- Optional launch, disconnect, or lock-up clutches;
- Sensors measuring vehicle speed, motor speed, wheel speed, torque, battery state of charge, temperature, road grade, and accelerator/brake position;
- Actuators that adjust the CVT ratio and clutch state; and
- A supervisory controller containing motor-efficiency maps, inverter-loss maps, CVT-efficiency maps, battery-power limits, and vehicle-resistance models.

The CVT may be belt-and-pulley, chain, traction-drive, hydrostatic, electric-variable, or another ratio-continuously-variable device. In some implementations, the CVT also provides a fixed-ratio or direct-drive state to reduce transmission losses.

## Coordinated control method

For each control interval, the controller may:

1. Determine the wheel torque and wheel speed needed to satisfy driver demand.
2. Identify feasible combinations of motor torque, motor speed, and CVT ratio that produce the requested wheel output.
3. Estimate total battery power for each combination, including:
   - Motor and inverter losses;
   - CVT losses;
   - Battery internal losses;
   - Auxiliary loads; and
   - Energy required to move or clamp the CVT.
4. Apply constraints such as motor-speed limits, battery current limits, component temperatures, traction limits, ratio slew rate, and drivability requirements.
5. Select the combination that minimizes battery energy consumption or maximizes recovered energy.
6. Command motor torque and CVT ratio along coordinated trajectories to avoid torque disturbances.

A simplified optimization objective can be expressed as:

\[
\min_{T_m,\omega_m,r} P_{\text{battery}}
\]

subject to:

\[
T_w \approx T_m\,r\,\eta_{\text{CVT}}, \qquad
\omega_m \approx r\,\omega_w
\]

and applicable motor, battery, transmission, and traction constraints.

The controller can include predicted road grade, traffic, route speed, and navigation data. Model-predictive control may select current and future CVT ratios to minimize expected trip energy rather than merely optimizing the present operating point.

## Example operating modes

### 1. Efficiency-optimized cruise mode

During steady cruising, the CVT selects a ratio that places the motor near a high-efficiency speed-and-torque region. At higher vehicle speeds, the transmission may use an overdrive ratio to reduce motor speed and associated iron, windage, and inverter-switching losses.

### 2. Acceleration or high-torque mode

For launch, passing, or hill climbing, the CVT selects a lower ratio that multiplies wheel torque. This allows the motor to produce the required wheel force without excessive motor current. As vehicle speed rises, the ratio changes continuously while motor torque is coordinated to provide smooth acceleration.

### 3. Economy acceleration mode

When maximum performance is unnecessary, motor torque and CVT ratio are scheduled so the motor follows an efficient operating path. The system may intentionally use moderate motor torque over a longer period if that consumes less battery energy than a high-current launch.

### 4. Regenerative-braking mode

During deceleration, the CVT selects a ratio that keeps motor speed and regenerative torque within efficient and allowable regions. Coordination may:

- Maximize recovered electrical energy;
- Prevent motor overspeed;
- Respect battery charge-power and state-of-charge limits;
- Blend regeneration with friction braking; and
- Maintain stable wheel slip.

If the battery cannot accept additional energy, the ratio may be changed to reduce regeneration, or friction braking may provide the remaining deceleration.

### 5. Coasting or sail mode

When little or no wheel torque is requested, the controller may command near-zero motor torque and select a low-drag CVT ratio. If a disconnect clutch is present, the motor and transmission may be decoupled from the wheels to reduce rotational losses. The system can choose between true coasting and mild regeneration based on route and traffic conditions.

### 6. Direct-drive or CVT lock-up mode

Where transmission ratio variation provides little benefit, a clutch or locking mechanism may establish a mechanically efficient fixed ratio. This reduces belt clamping, hydraulic, or traction-drive losses. The controller exits lock-up when additional torque multiplication or motor-speed optimization is advantageous.

### 7. Thermal-management or component-protection mode

If the motor, inverter, battery, or CVT approaches a thermal limit, the controller changes ratio to shift losses away from the constrained component. For example, it may increase motor speed and reduce torque to lower current-related heating, or reduce motor speed to limit iron losses.

### 8. Low-traction mode

On snow, ice, or loose surfaces, the system limits wheel torque and ratio-change rate. Motor torque and CVT ratio are coordinated to avoid abrupt torque multiplication, while wheel-slip feedback adjusts the commands.

### 9. Limp-home or fault mode

If ratio control, a sensor, or a clutch fails, the transmission may be held at a safe ratio while motor torque is derated. If available, a fixed-ratio bypass or lock-up path can permit continued operation.

## Range-improvement mechanisms

Range can improve through:

- Keeping the motor and inverter near their peak-efficiency operating regions;
- Reducing high-current operation during launch and climbing;
- Lowering motor speed during highway cruising;
- Increasing usable regenerative braking over a wider range of vehicle speeds;
- Enabling low-drag coasting or disconnection;
- Selecting direct drive when CVT losses exceed the benefit of ratio optimization; and
- Using route prediction to avoid unnecessary acceleration, braking, and ratio changes.

Because a CVT introduces its own mechanical and actuation losses, the controller should optimize total battery-to-wheel efficiency rather than motor efficiency alone. In some conditions, the most efficient strategy is to hold or lock the CVT ratio even though another ratio would improve motor efficiency. Coordinated, mode-dependent control is therefore central to achieving a net range benefit.

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a concise patent abstract for an EV powertrain controller capable of simultaneously controlling motor current and CVT ratio to optimize subsystem efficiencies.
counterfactuals.output: An electric vehicle powertrain controller coordinates motor current and continuously variable transmission (CVT) ratio to improve overall powertrain efficiency. The controller receives a requested wheel torque and operating parameters of the motor, CVT, and vehicle, and determines a motor-current command and a CVT-ratio command by optimizing combined subsystem losses while satisfying torque, speed, voltage, current, ratio, and drivability constraints. The commands are updated concurrently in response to changing operating conditions, enabling the motor and CVT to operate near respective high-efficiency regions without compromising requested vehicle performance.
